cover.headline: India's cleanest mortgage book, priced for returns it does not earn: a 12-13% ROE lender at 3x book, with an 11.7% stake sale still to come. We initiate at HOLD.
cover.lead: Bajaj Housing Finance (BHFL) is India's largest non-deposit-taking housing-finance company: ₹1.50 lakh cr of home loans, loans against property, lease-rental and developer loans, AAA-funded, with gross bad loans of just 0.29% and loan losses of 5-20bp a year. It grows 21-24% a year. The problem is the economics: prime home loans are priced by banks, margins are falling (NIM −20-25bp guided for FY27), and return on equity is 12-13%, barely above our 12.5% cost of equity. The street values the stock on **P/B on FY28E book (2.5-2.7x)**. We forecast EPS of ₹3.58 / ₹4.23 / ₹4.99 for FY27-29E and ROE of {{F.roe.0|pct}}-{{F.roe.2|pct}}. Applying **2.1x to Sep-28E book of ₹37.3** (the stock's own 2.5x median over the last year, adjusted for the −15% move in housing-finance multiples) gives **{{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}): HOLD, at the edge of SELL.** Our intrinsic checks are lower still (justified P/B ₹52, residual income ₹44): at ₹82 the market prices a long-run ROE of ~{{dcf.impliedRoe|pct0}}. Bull {{scen.bull.tp|inr}}; bear {{scen.bear.tp|inr}}.

arguments.h: A superb mortgage franchise: fast, clean and cheap to run
arguments.p: AUM +24% in Q1FY27 with a record ₹8,918 cr added; gross NPA 0.29%, nil in lease-rental loans since inception; loan losses 17bp in FY26 and guided at 10-15bp; opex only 19.6% of income with 2,025 staff. Funding is AAA with a positive behavioural maturity gap. On quality there is little to criticise.

arguments.h: But it earns a utility return: ROE 12-13% against a 12.5% cost of equity
arguments.p: Prime home loans are priced by SBI and the private banks; NIM fell from 3.9% to 3.7% in a year and management expects 6-10bp more. ROE was 12.1% in FY26 and is guided at 12-13% for FY27; it rises only if leverage goes from 5.8x toward the 8x ceiling. We model {{F.roe.0|pct}} → {{F.roe.2|pct}}. A lender earning its cost of capital is worth about book; BHFL trades at 3.0x.

arguments.h: The parent must still sell ~₹8,000 cr of stock
arguments.p: Bajaj Finance holds 86.70% and must get to 75% by 15-Sep-2029 (deadline extended in Mar-2026). That is 97.5 cr shares, ~₹7,994 cr at ₹82: 0.9x today's free float and ~174 days of average trading. The first 2% (Dec-2025) knocked 9% off the price. Institutions own under 2%; 23 lakh retail holders own 11%.

arguments.h: Valuation: de-rated from 6.1x to 2.4x forward book, still the priciest HFC
arguments.p: The forward P/B fell from 6.1x at listing to 2.4x (FY28E), and the stock trades 17% above its ₹70 IPO price. Yet at 3.0x trailing book it is still the dearest listed housing-finance company (next: Home First Finance at 2.7x with a 16% ROE) on the lowest FY26 ROE in the group (12.1%). Our 2.1x Sep-28E book gives {{dcf.tp|inr}}; a 2.5x multiple (its 12-month median) gives ~₹93.

catalysts: Q2FY27 results (due by mid-November 2026): management will raise FY27 AUM guidance only if the Q1 easing in balance-transfer attrition holds for another quarter.
The parent's next sell-down tranche: size, price and route (block deals, an offer for sale, or a fresh BHFL issue). The Dec-2025 block took 9% off the price.
Bajaj Finance's own equity raise (board meeting noticed for early October 2026): if it raises enough, it has less reason to rush BHFL sales.
The rate cycle: management says rate cuts are over; a repo hike would let it reprice ~₹17,000 cr of repo-linked loans and its lending rate, the only route to wider margins.
Sambhav (near-prime and affordable) reaching ₹600 cr+ of monthly disbursements and 20% of home loans by Mar-27: the one yield lever management controls.

sections.title: A full-range mortgage lender: home loans for salaried Indians, plus rent-backed loans to landlords and builders

blocks.p: Bajaj Housing Finance (BHFL) is a housing-finance company (HFC) owned 86.7% by Bajaj Finance, registered with the National Housing Bank and treated by the RBI as an "upper-layer" NBFC, the tier with bank-like rules. It is India's largest HFC that does not take deposits and the second largest HFC overall after LIC Housing Finance. It lends only against property. In FY26 it earned ₹10,512 cr of interest and ₹639 cr of fees and other income (insurance commissions, charges, and income on loans it sold), paid ₹6,760 cr of interest, spent ₹867 cr on operations and set aside ₹191 cr for bad loans, leaving ₹3,320 cr of pre-tax profit.

The arithmetic is thin. In Q1FY27 the loan book yielded 8.9% and funding cost 7.2%, a gross spread of 1.7 percentage points. Equity-funded loans and fee income lift the net interest margin to 3.7% of loans. From that, operating costs take ~0.7% and bad loans ~0.05-0.2%, leaving a return on assets of 2.3%. A ~6x leverage turns that into a 12-13% return on equity. Every one of those numbers is good for a mortgage lender; together they are still a modest business.

blocks.p: Distribution is lean: 224 branches in 182 locations across 20 states and union territories, 2,025 employees (Jun-2026), centralised underwriting hubs, ~95% of retail applications and agreements digital. Home loans come through developers whose projects BHFL has approved (9,800+ projects) and finances, through direct-selling agents and connectors, and through digital partners. Lease-rental and developer loans are sold relationship by relationship to 332 landlords and 608 developers. In 2024 BHFL added "Sambhav", a separate unit for near-prime and affordable home loans (ticket ~₹28 lakh, target yields 9-13%), now disbursing ₹450-465 cr a month.

blocks.callout: **Why this matters:** BHFL is two businesses in one balance sheet. The retail half (home loans and LAP, 64% of AUM) is a scale business where banks set the price and BHFL competes on speed and service. The commercial half (lease-rental and developer loans, 35%) carries higher yields per rupee of cost and has had no losses, but it is lumpy, concentrated (an average lease-rental loan is ₹137 cr) and capped by the rule that half of an HFC's assets must be individual home loans.

sections.title: Built in eight years on ~₹13,100 cr of parent and IPO equity; listed because the RBI required it

blocks.p: BHFL started lending in FY18 as Bajaj Finance's mortgage arm. It grew AUM from ₹3,570 cr to ₹1,40,706 cr in eight years, funded by ₹9,200 cr of equity from the parent (FY18-FY25, incl. a ₹2,000 cr rights issue in Apr-2024; ₹328 cr more before FY18), a ₹3,560 cr IPO fresh issue, and retained profit. The listing was not optional: the RBI classed BHFL as an "upper-layer" NBFC in FY23, which requires a stock-market listing within three years. The IPO in Sep-2024 drew record demand (63.6x subscribed) and set a valuation the stock has been unwinding ever since.

sections.title: Housing finance in India: a long runway, a slow year, and banks that set the price

blocks.p: India's home-loan market is large and under-penetrated, but it is not growing fast right now. The industry's individual home loans grew only 9.4% in FY26 against the 11-12% BHFL normally expects, and management sees 9-10.5% in FY27: after two years in which buyers rushed to lock in rising property prices, prices have stopped rising and purchases are being postponed, a "stabilisation phase" in the MD's words (Q1FY27 call). BHFL grows 2x the market by taking share, not because the market is booming.

Prime home loans are a bank product. Banks fund them with cheap current and savings deposits that an HFC cannot take, so they set the price and HFCs follow: "in the prime housing we exactly compete with all the banks including SBI, HDFC" (MD, Q4FY26 call). About 20% of BHFL's home-loan book leaves every year, half of it refinanced away by other lenders (balance transfers), mostly to public-sector banks. That is why every listed housing-finance company has drifted toward higher-yield niches: loans against property, affordable housing, construction finance.

blocks.callout: **Our view:** demand is not BHFL's constraint; price and regulation are. In prime home loans it competes with lenders that have a structurally cheaper liability, so its margin on that half of the book will stay thin. It earns more on lease-rental, developer and near-prime loans, but the 50% individual-housing floor (it is at 50.45%) caps how far it can tilt the balance sheet toward them.

blocks.callout: **Our view:** the trends that help BHFL (commercial real estate, efficiency, parentage) mostly protect returns rather than raise them, and the ones that hurt (bank competition, the end of the rate-cut cycle, the housing-share floor) act on its biggest product. That is why we model ROE rising only slowly, from {{F.roe.0|pct}} to {{F.roe.2|pct}}, and only because leverage rises.

sections.title: Retail: a prime home-loan machine that wins on speed, not price; Sambhav is the yield lever

blocks.p: Home loans (₹80,865 cr, 54% of AUM) are the core: prime borrowers, an average ticket of ₹48.9 lakh at origination, 83% salaried, 78% with a credit score above 750. BHFL wins business through builders whose projects it has approved and often financed (9,800+ approved projects), through agents and digital partners, and on turnaround time. It does not win on price; it matches the banks. Home loans grew 18% in FY26 and 20% in Q1FY27, below the company as a whole, because of the ~20% annual attrition. Loans against property (₹15,445 cr) are prime, high-ticket (₹91.6 lakh), 79% to self-employed borrowers and 70% against self-occupied homes; 15% of the book is "flexi" (a drawable limit).

blocks.p: **Sambhav** is BHFL's near-prime and affordable unit, launched in 2024 with its own sales and underwriting teams. It now lends ₹450-465 cr a month (₹325-350 cr two quarters earlier), at an average ticket of ₹28 lakh, two-thirds near-prime (target yield 9-11%) and one-third affordable (11-13%), with 65% of borrowers above a 750 credit score. Management wants ₹600 cr+ a month within nine months and the prime : Sambhav mix of home loans to move from 84 : 16 to 80 : 20 by Mar-27. It is the one lever that lifts yields without taking construction risk, but the book is young (most loans are under 12 months old) and its credit costs have not been tested.

sections.title: Lease-rental and developer loans: a third of the book, zero losses so far, and big tickets

blocks.p: **Lease rental discounting (LRD, ₹34,604 cr, 23% of AUM)** lends against the contracted rent of completed offices, warehouses and industrial parks: the tenant pays rent into an escrow account and the lender takes its instalment first. BHFL has 332 such customers with an average loan of ₹137 cr at origination; 68% are REITs, sovereign and pension funds, MNC funds, large companies and large developers. It has had no bad loans since inception. LRD grew 44% in FY26 and 41% in Q1FY27, making it the main source of growth. The MD groups it with home loans as "lower margin" than developer loans, but the cost of servicing a ₹137 cr loan per rupee is tiny.

**Developer finance (₹17,002 cr, 11%)** funds the construction of residential and commercial projects for 608 developers across 895 projects (average ₹58.8 cr), released in tranches against construction milestones, with sales receipts swept through escrow and interest paid from day one. It is the highest-margin product in the book (MD, Q4FY26 call) and a feeder for retail home loans. Growth slowed to 13% in FY26 and 19% in Q1FY27 because funded projects are repaying faster. One account moved to Stage 3 in Q1FY27 (gross NPA 0.12%); it was already provided at ~48%.

blocks.callout: **The honest risk:** the commercial book has never been through a property downturn under BHFL. LRD depends on tenants renewing leases and on office values; developer loans on project sales. Both are secured and escrowed, and BHFL picks large, rated counterparties, but tickets of ₹60-140 cr mean a handful of defaults would move credit costs from ~10bp to 30-50bp. Our bear case adds 10bp; a real commercial-property slump would cost more.

sections.title: NIM: down 20-25bp this year as the old book runs off; banks leave no room to reprice

blocks.p: BHFL's reported net interest margin (net total income ÷ average loan assets) was 3.9% in FY26 and 3.7% in Q1FY27. Management expects FY27 to be 20-25bp below FY26, of which 14bp is already in Q1 and "6 bps to 10 bps" more is to come. The reason is mechanical: in a stable-rate market the old book, written at higher rates, keeps repaying and is replaced by new loans at today's lower acquisition rates. The 2025 rate cuts were passed through to ~₹17,000 cr of repo-linked loans and to the lending rate (another 15bp in Dec-2025). Funding costs fell more slowly (7.9% in Q4FY25 → 7.2% in Q1FY27) and the incremental money-market rate rose in Q4-Q1. The CFO's summary: "largely it will still have compression because of the yields going down".

blocks.p: **Rates: which way helps?** Counter-intuitively, BHFL's margin would benefit from a rate *hike*. 63% of its borrowings are floating (including swaps), so its funding cost rises with rates, but so do its repo-linked loans and its lending rate; management says that in a hike "it has never happened that there is no pass-through", typically 10-20bp of a 25bp move, and that without a hike it cannot pass on dearer money-market funding. In a long pause, competition grinds yields down; that is the scenario management assumes for FY27, and so do we.

blocks.callout: **Our forecast:** net total income ÷ average AUM falls from {{fin.ntiPct.6|pct}} in FY26 to {{F.ntiPct.0|pct}} in FY27E (≈3.65% on loan assets, slightly below the ~3.7% management guides) and {{F.ntiPct.2|pct}} by FY29E: yields drift down a few basis points a year while the Sambhav mix and a slightly lower cost of funds offset part of it, and rising leverage means more of the book is debt-funded. We do not assume the margin recovery that Emkay (NIM up in FY28-29E) builds in.

sections.title: Asset quality: among the cleanest books in Indian lending, with a commercial tail risk

blocks.p: Gross bad loans (Stage 3) were 0.29% of loans in Jun-2026 and net 0.12%, in a 0.26-0.30% range for nine quarters; Stage 2 (30-90 days overdue) was 0.32%. Loan losses have been 6-17bp of average loans for three years (FY24-FY26), and 5bp annualised in Q1FY27. That Q1 figure flatters: a ~₹2,300 cr loan sale released Stage 1 provisions and the January model recalibration lowered Stage 1 rates after two clean years. Management guides 10-15bp for FY27. By product, home loans run at 0.34% gross NPA, loans against property at 0.62% (normal range 50-70bp), developer loans at 0.12% (one account) and lease-rental loans at zero.

blocks.p: **Why losses are so low:** prime salaried borrowers with high credit scores, collateral worth well above the loan, centralised underwriting with tele/video interviews for every salaried loan, and, in the commercial book, escrowed cash flows from rated tenants and milestone-based releases to builders. Provisions held (₹740 cr in Jun-2026, 0.56% of loans) are small in absolute terms, but so is the problem they cover. The two things that could change the picture are an untested Sambhav book (young loans to near-prime and affordable borrowers) and the commercial property book (big tickets).

Credit cost barely matters to the valuation: each 5bp is ~2.1% of FY28E profit. Margin is what matters. The bear case adds 10bp across the board (a commercial-property shock), which still leaves losses below most lenders' good years.

sections.title: Funding: AAA, long-dated and diversified, but still dearer than a bank's deposits

blocks.p: BHFL funds itself like a top-rated corporate. In Jun-2026 its ₹1.1 lakh cr of borrowings were 46.5% bonds (NCDs), 38.3% bank loans from 18 banks, 9.9% refinance from the National Housing Bank and 5.3% commercial paper; in FY26 it added floating-rate pass-through certificates. Long-term debt is rated AAA/Stable by CRISIL and India Ratings. It borrows mostly for 3-5 years, so its liabilities mature after its assets on a behavioural basis: the cumulative surplus is positive in every bucket up to one year. The liquidity buffer is small (₹2,516 cr) but the liquidity coverage ratio was 158% against the 100% required. Cost of funds was 7.2% in Q1FY27, 50bp lower than a year earlier.

blocks.callout: **Why it matters:** housing-finance companies fail on funding, not on credit (DHFL, 2019). BHFL's funding is as good as a non-bank's gets: AAA, long-dated, diversified and backed by a strong parent. It is not a cost advantage over banks, which fund home loans with deposits costing far less; that is the root of the margin problem.

sections.title: Capital: plenty for now; ROE rises only by spending it

blocks.p: Capital adequacy was 21.59% in Jun-2026 (Tier 1 21.17%) against a 15% minimum; total assets were 5.8x equity against an internal ceiling of 8x and guidance of 5.8-6.3x for FY27. BHFL has never paid a dividend. With the ₹5,560 cr raised in FY25 still being deployed, it has spare capital, and that is precisely why ROE is low: ROA of ~2.2% on loan assets times ~5.6x leverage is ~12%. The path to a higher ROE runs through more leverage, not better margins.

The next raise, probably early in the 2030s, could double as the route to the 25% public float: a fresh issue to outside investors dilutes the parent without the parent selling. That option is not in our numbers and has not been announced.

sections.title: Profit up 41% a year since FY21, but returns peaked in FY24 and growth is settling near 18%

blocks.p: Bajaj Housing Finance grew net profit from ₹453 cr in FY21 to ₹2,560 cr in FY26 (41% a year) and its loan book (AUM) from ₹38,871 cr to ₹1,40,706 cr (29% a year). Profit grew faster than the book for three reasons: operating costs fell from 28% of net income to 20% as the business scaled, loan losses fell from 0.8% of loans (FY21, Covid) to under 0.2%, and leverage rose. Those tailwinds are now used up. Return on equity peaked at 15.2% in FY24, fell to 13.4% in FY25 when ₹5,560 cr of new equity arrived (rights issue and IPO) and to 12.1% in FY26 as margins narrowed. FY26 profit grew 18%; we forecast 17-18% a year for FY27-29E.

From here profit growth depends on AUM growth (21-23%) minus margin erosion (NIM down 20-25bp in FY27). That is why we forecast EPS growth of {{F.epsGrowth.0|pct}} / {{F.epsGrowth.1|pct}} / {{F.epsGrowth.2|pct}} for FY27-29E, below AUM growth, with ROE edging up only as leverage rises ({{F.roe.0|pct}} → {{F.roe.2|pct}}).

sections.title: The parent must sell ~₹8,000 cr of stock by Sep-2029; the market has to absorb it

blocks.p: Indian rules require every listed company to have at least 25% of its shares with the public. BHFL listed with Bajaj Finance holding 88.75%. The parent sold ~2% in a bulk deal on 2-Dec-2025 (16.66 cr shares, stake now 86.70%); the stock fell 9% that day to a then-record low of ₹94.90. In March 2026 a change to the Securities Contracts Rules moved BHFL's deadline from Sep-2027 to **15-Sep-2029**. Bajaj Finance has said: "We will go down to 75%, while we have time and we are in no hurry. First protocol most likely will be BHFL dilution" (30-Jul-2026). Eight weeks later it put its own equity raise to its board, which suggests it does not need BHFL cash urgently.

blocks.p: **What it does to the share price.** Supply of this size usually comes at a discount (block deals and offers for sale are priced below market), and every tranche resets the price for the next. Over the long run a bigger float is a positive: index providers weight by free float, so BHFL's weight in indices would roughly double at 25% public, and institutions could own more of it. But the near-term arithmetic is unfriendly: the stock needs ~₹8,000 cr of new buyers over three years at a time when foreign and domestic funds together own under 2%. We see the overhang as one reason the stock trades below its own history; we do not see it as a reason for the multiple to recover.

blocks.callout: **Consistency with our Bajaj Finance report:** that report (same date) assumed BFL sells down to 75% in two tranches by H1FY28 at ₹82, adding the after-tax gain to BFL's equity and a larger minority interest to its accounts. The deadline is in fact 15-Sep-2029 (confirmed in BHFL's FY26 annual report), so the sale can be slower; the amount (~11.7%) is the same. For BHFL's own shareholders, a secondary sale changes nothing in the business; a fresh issue would add capital BHFL does not need yet and cut its ROE. **Our base case assumes secondary sales and no new BHFL shares.**

blocks.callout: **Honest verdict:** BHFL is a high-quality franchise without a moat that shows up in returns. Against other housing-finance companies it wins on funding, underwriting and cost; against banks, which own prime home loans, it has no edge in price. The result is a business that grows fast and safely and earns roughly its cost of capital. Quality of that kind deserves a premium to book, but not the ~3x the stock trades at.

blocks.p: Q1FY27 (Apr-Jun 2026) was strong on volume: AUM +24% to ₹1,49,624 cr with a record ₹8,918 cr added (₹5,736 cr a year earlier), disbursements +33% to ₹19,509 cr, PAT +23% to ₹715 cr, ROE 12.5%. With loan losses at a normal 10-15bp, profit would have grown ~20%, in line with our FY27E. sections.title: Earnings quality: clean books; loan sales to the parent and up-front gains deserve a look

blocks.p: We rate accounting **AMBER**, leaning green. The joint auditors (Mukund M. Chitale & Co. and Singhi & Co.) gave an unmodified FY26 opinion; products are simple; BHFL recognises interest only from the day a cheque is encashed (it has done so for six years, before the regulator asked lenders to); and asset quality leaves little room for provisioning games. Four points deserve attention:

bullets: **Loan sales to the parent.** BHFL sold ₹3,645 cr of loans to Bajaj Finance in FY26 and keeps servicing them for a fee (₹25 cr received). Its 2026 AGM sought omnibus approval for up to ₹12,500 cr of such transfers. They are described as arm's length and they help BHFL stay above the 50% housing-share floor, but the buyer is the controlling shareholder, and pricing is not disclosed.

**Up-front gains on assignments.** When BHFL sells a pool and keeps the excess interest, Ind AS lets it book the present value of that spread at once. "Income on derecognised (assigned) loans" was ₹195 cr in FY26 (₹144 cr in FY25), ~6% of pre-tax profit; together with sale of services it was ₹216 cr. Lumpy assignment quarters (Q1FY27: ~₹2,300 cr) lift fees and, by releasing Stage 1 provisions, cut credit cost.

**Model recalibration.** Expected-loss rates are recalibrated every January; after two clean years Stage 1 rates came down, which is why Stage 1 provisions stayed at ₹401 cr while Stage 1 loans grew ₹7,400 cr in Q1FY27. Reasonable, but it means provisions are cyclically low.
**One-offs both ways.** Q4FY25 had a ₹34 cr tax credit (FY26 PAT growth 18% reported, 20% without it); FY26 had a ₹13 cr Labour Code charge. Small.

blocks.p: **What would justify today's price on fundamentals?** On Sep-27E book, ₹82 is 2.51x. In the justified-P/B formula that needs a cost of equity of 11.6% with a 14% long-run ROE, or 12.0% with 15%, against our 12.5%, and a 10% growth rate held for ever. That is not absurd: a AAA mortgage book with 0.3% bad loans arguably deserves a lower cost of equity than a consumer lender. But a 14-15% ROE needs 7-8x leverage on today's margins, and it has to last for decades. The price assumes the optimistic end on every input, which is why we would not buy here.

sections.title: Our honest summary: a great lender, a full price, and a parent with stock to sell

blocks.callout: **What you are buying:** India's cleanest large mortgage book (gross NPA 0.29%, nil losses in lease-rental loans), 21-24% growth, opex at 20% of income, AAA funding, strong parentage and management that meets its guidance. Profit compounds at ~17-18% a year and book value at ~13-14%.

**What you are paying:** 3.0x trailing book and 2.4x our FY28E book for a 12.4-13.4% ROE against a 12.5% cost of equity. That is the highest P/B of any listed housing-finance company, with the lowest ROE. The street's method, at our derived multiple, gives {{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}), a HOLD at the edge of SELL; our justified P/B (₹52) and residual income (₹44) are 35-45% below the price. On top, the parent must place ~₹7,994 cr of stock by Sep-2029.

Sources: Q1FY27 investor presentation (29-Jul-2026, incl. the FY27 management assessment) and call transcript (call 29-Jul-2026, filed 4-Aug-2026); Q4FY26 presentation (27-Apr-2026) and call; Annual Report FY2025-26 (notice dated 4-Jul-2026); Screener.in standalone statements (FY20 column repaired by BAJAJHFL.patch.js). All drivers are on AUM, which includes the ~12% of loans assigned off the balance sheet, so yields and margins read lower than the company's ratios on loan assets (AR).

history._why: Company 9-year snapshot (Q1FY27 presentation p10): closing AUM, loan losses & provisions, and 'fees and other income' (fees and commission, fair-value gains, sale of services and income on derecognised (assigned) loans, other). Revenue = interest income + fees ties to Screener within ₹16 cr in every year; FY26 ties to ₹1 cr.

src.all: Q1FY27 investor presentation p10 (9-year financial snapshot), 29-Jul-2026; FY25-FY26 also p22 and Annual Report FY2025-26 MD&A table 1(a)

assumptions._baseWhy: 833.23 cr equity shares in issue at 31-Mar-2026 (Annual Report FY2025-26, directors' report: ₹8,332.33 cr paid-up at ₹10 face value, after 41.9 lakh ESOP shares allotted to the ESOP trust in FY26); Motilal Oswal and Emkay also use 8,332 mn. Screener's FY26 EPS (₹3.07, rounded) implies 833.9 cr; Screener's equity capital (₹8,329 cr) nets ~0.3 cr shares held by the ESOP trust. The 0.1% gap is rounding.
assumptions._aumGrowthWhy: FY27 management assessment (29-Jul-2026): 21-23%. Q1FY27 added a record ₹8,918 cr (₹5,736 cr a year earlier); four more such quarters would be +25%, and balance-transfer (BT-out) attrition eased in Q1. We take the top of guidance for FY27 and fade 2pp a year: the home-loan industry grew only 9.4% in FY26, prime home loans compete head-on with banks, and individual home loans are already at 50.45% of assets vs the 50% regulatory floor (Mar-26), which caps how fast lease-rental and developer loans can grow on the balance sheet. Street: Motilal Oswal ~25% FY27E, Emkay 23.5/24/23.5%, JM Financial 22.3/22.6%.
assumptions._yieldOnAumWhy: Interest income ÷ average AUM: 8.72% FY25, 8.23% FY26, 7.87% annualised in Q1FY27 (portfolio yield 8.9% vs 9.5% a year earlier). Management: the old, higher-yield book keeps running off and is replaced at lower acquisition rates in a stable-rate regime; NIM (on loan assets) to fall 20-25bp in FY27 vs FY26, of which 14bp came in Q1 and '6-10 bps' more is expected. Partly offset by the Sambhav (near-prime and affordable) mix rising from 16% to 20% of home loans (target yield 9-13% vs prime). We take 2bp more off in Q2-Q4 and 3-7bp a year after.
assumptions._feeIncomePctWhy: Fees and other income ÷ average AUM: 0.55% FY25, 0.50% FY26, 0.57% annualised in Q1FY27 (lifted by income on a ~₹2,300 cr assignment; insurance commissions rising with disbursements). Assignments stay at 12-13% of AUM (CFO), so assignment income grows with the book.
assumptions._costOfFundsWhy: Interest expense ÷ average year-end borrowings: 7.91% FY25, 7.28% FY26, ~7.05% annualised in Q1FY27 (company basis 7.2%, down 7bp QoQ; 63% of borrowings floating incl. swaps). Management: Q2 'sideways with a downward bias'; incremental money-market funding was dearer in Q4-Q1 and 'the scenario of a cut of rate is over'. We hold it near the Q1 level.
assumptions._opexPctWhy: Opex incl. depreciation ÷ average AUM: 0.72% FY25, 0.68% FY26, 0.63% annualised in Q1FY27. Guidance: opex to net total income 19-20% (FY26 19.7%, Q1 19.6%), 'sideways' because NIM falls while efficiency improves (AI underwriting, centralised hubs). Our values give ~19.6% / 19.3% / 18.9% cost-to-income for FY27-29E.
assumptions._creditCostWhy: Provisions ÷ average AUM: 0.06% FY25 (incl. a ₹60 cr overlay release), 0.15% FY26 (incl. stronger Stage 2 cover), 0.04% annualised in Q1FY27 (Stage 1 release on a ₹2,300 cr assignment). Guidance: 10-15bp of average loan assets in FY27 = ~9-13bp of AUM. We take the middle for FY27 and edge up as Sambhav (near-prime/affordable) and LAP grow and the young books season. Street: Motilal Oswal 13/14bp of loans FY27/28E.
assumptions._taxRateWhy: Effective rate 22.9% FY26 and 23.0% in Q1FY27 (Screener); special reserve deduction (Section 36(1)(viii)) keeps it below the 25.2% statutory rate.
assumptions._payoutWhy: BHFL has never paid a dividend (Screener payout 0% FY20-FY26); it retains everything to fund 20%+ growth. A maiden dividend would lower book growth but not value.
assumptions._otherIncomeWhy: Non-operating items are negligible: Screener other income ₹-2 cr FY25 and ₹-14 cr FY26 (a ₹13 cr Labour Code exceptional charge). We assume none.
assumptions._capitalRaiseWhy: No primary equity needed: CRAR 21.59% (Tier 1 21.17%) in Jun-2026 vs a 15% minimum, leverage 5.8x vs an internal ceiling of 8x. The parent's sell-down to 75% (deadline 15-Sep-2029) is a secondary sale: it changes who owns BHFL, not BHFL's equity. A fresh issue to meet the float rule is possible but not announced; see the capital chapter.

valuation._why: Ke = 6.5% + 1.0 × 6% = 12.5% (house rf and ERP; beta 1.0: a low-credit-risk AAA mortgage book, offset by 6x leverage, rate sensitivity and a float overhang; two years of trading history is too short for a statistical beta). sustainableRoe 14% = ROA of 2.0-2.2% on loan assets (management's medium-term range) at 6.5-7x leverage, well inside the 8x internal ceiling; it has never been above 15.2% (FY24). g = 10% long-run book growth in the justified P/B (about nominal GDP; the book grows faster than that for several years, which the residual-income check captures). Residual income: ROE fades from FY29E to 14% over 8 years, payout rising to 30%, 6% terminal growth.

methods.name: P/B
methods.why: The street's method (Motilal Oswal 2.7x FY28E, Emkay 2.6x FY28E, JM Financial 2.5x FY28E at initiation). 2.1x = BHFL's own median forward P/B over the last 12 months (2.5x; the same since the parent's first sell-down in Dec-2025) × the housing-finance sector's move against its own last-12-month medians on 30-Sep-2026 (−15%: median of seven listed HFCs). The since-listing median (3.7x) is not used on its own: the first year priced an IPO scarcity premium (63.6x subscription, stock at 2.6x the issue price). Bull 2.5x = BHFL's 12-month median (sector back to its recent norm); bear 1.6x = justified P/B at a 14% ROE, about where listed affordable-housing lenders trade.

methods.name: Justified P/B
methods.why: (ROE − g) ÷ (Ke − g) = (14 − 10) ÷ (12.5 − 10) = 1.6x book at the 12-month target date.

methods.name: Residual income
methods.why: Book plus the present value of profit above the 12.5% cost of equity, ROE fading to 14%, rolled forward 6 months.

methods.name: P/E
methods.why: Cross-check only, derived the same way: BHFL's median forward P/E over the last 12 months (20.7x) × the HFC sector's P/E move against its 12-month medians (−17%) = 17x. Bull 20.5x = the 12-month median; bear 12.5x = the median trailing P/E of seven listed HFCs.

bull.label: Bull
bull.narrative: BT-out keeps easing and Sambhav reaches 20%+ of home loans: AUM +25/23/22%, yield +5bp, opex 2bp lower (AI, scale), credit cost 3bp lower (the FY24-25 run-rate); leverage climbs toward 7x and long-run ROE reaches 16%.

bear.label: Bear
bear.narrative: Banks keep cutting prime home-loan rates and the commercial book slows (AUM +18/16/15%), yield −15bp, and a commercial real-estate downturn lifts credit cost by 10bp (to ~0.2-0.25% of AUM, still low); long-run ROE stays at 12%.
